plan.topic: Tirzepatide vs insulin degludec in type 2 diabetes: the SURPASS-3 randomized head-to-head (Lancet 2021, adults with type 2 diabetes on metformin with or without an SGLT2 inhibitor, 52 weeks)
plan.angle: Open: 'In adults with type 2 diabetes already on metformin, tirzepatide lowered A1C more than a long-acting insulin over a year. Weight went down on tirzepatide and up a little on insulin.' Give the A1C (% and mmol/mol) and weight change as a dose range for tirzepatide vs degludec, measured 'if everyone stayed on treatment', with per-arm n on screen. Add GI rates and low blood sugar rates exactly as the Lancet paper reports them. Honesty line: 'One open-label, company-funded trial, type 2 diabetes only. Insulin is still essential for many people.' Close: 'Bigger average isn't best for everyone. Don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own. Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.' Optional save/share line. No 'follow for more'. 170 words or fewer.
plan.working_title: Tirzepatide vs Insulin for Type 2 Diabetes #shorts
plan.why:
Tirzepatide-first head-to-heads have a median of 106 (signal, n=5). This one uses a new trial, so it follows the variety rule, and it brings in type 2 diabetes searchers. | fact-check: SURPASS-3 (Ludvik et al., Lancet 2021) is a real randomized, open-label, Lilly-funded 52-week trial of tirzepatide 5/10/15 mg vs titrated insulin degludec in adults with type 2 diabetes on metformin ± SGLT2 inhibitor. It's a legitimate new head-to-head for the lead slot. Fixes:
(1) The angle asks for 'the estimand'. Never say or show that word. Use 'if everyone stayed on treatment' (efficacy estimand) consistently for both arms.
(2) Three tirzepatide doses × A1C % × mmol/mol × weight × n won't fit in 170 words or on readable stat pills. Use the dose range ('across the three doses') with per-arm n on screen. Doses appear only as trial arm labels, never as guidance.
(3) Cut 'Follow for more.' Engagement lines ask to save or share only.
(4) Hypoglycaemia: quote the paper's threshold (<54 mg/dL or severe) and the per-arm rates exactly. Note it was lower on tirzepatide but present in both arms.
(5) GI rates per arm from the paper, briefly.
Keep 'insulin remains essential for many people', 'type 2 diabetes only', 'open-label, company-funded', and 'don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own'. Never imply that someone on insulin should ask to swap. Frame it as a question for the prescriber about the overall treatment plan.

package.title: Tirzepatide vs Insulin Degludec at 1 Year: The Trade-Off #shorts
package.description:
One-year SURPASS-3 trial in adults with type 2 diabetes on metformin: if everyone stayed on treatment, tirzepatide lowered A1C more than insulin degludec (about 1.9–2.4 vs about 1.3 points). Weight fell on tirzepatide and rose on insulin. The trade-off: more nausea (12–24% vs 2%).
One open-label, company-funded trial, type 2 diabetes only. Don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own. Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.
Source: Ludvik B et al., The Lancet 2021;398:583–598 (SURPASS-3) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34370970/
#Tirzepatide #TypeTwoDiabetes #SURPASS3 #GLP1 #InsulinDegludec

social.instagram_caption:
Metformin not enough anymore? That's the question behind the SURPASS-3 trial.

In this 52-week, open-label trial, adults with type 2 diabetes on metformin (with or without an SGLT2 inhibitor) were randomized to once-weekly tirzepatide or once-daily insulin degludec.

If everyone stayed on treatment:
• A1C fell about 1.9–2.4 points on tirzepatide vs about 1.3 on insulin
• Weight dropped 7.5 to almost 13 kg on tirzepatide vs a 2.3 kg rise on insulin

Side effects:
• Nausea: 12–24% on tirzepatide vs 2% on insulin (mostly mild to moderate)
• Low blood sugar (under 54 mg/dL or severe): 1–2% on tirzepatide vs 7% on insulin. Lower, but present in both

This is one open-label, company-funded trial in people with type 2 diabetes only. Insulin is still essential for many people, and a bigger average result isn't best for everyone.

Save this or share it with someone weighing options to discuss with their doctor.

factcheck.summary: All SURPASS-3 figures match the source. I checked them against Lilly Medical's SURPASS-3 results page, because the Lancet page returned 403 to the fetcher and PubMed showed only a cookie wall. A1C fell 1.93, 2.20 and 2.37 points on tirzepatide 5, 10 and 15 mg versus 1.34 on degludec. Weight changed by −7.5 to −12.9 kg on tirzepatide versus +2.3 kg on degludec. Nausea was 12%, 23% and 24% versus 2%. Glucose under 54 mg/dL or severe hypoglycaemia was 1%, 1% and 2% versus 7%. Group sizes were 358/360/359/360, and the efficacy measure assumes everyone stayed on treatment. The script describes the design correctly (randomized, open-label, Lilly-funded, 52 weeks, metformin with or without an SGLT2 inhibitor). It gives absolute rates and carries the caveats, the don't-switch line and the prescriber line. Narration is 170 words, right at the limit. There are only minor wording fixes.

issues.claim: Weight dropped seven and a half to almost thirteen kilos on tirzepatide. It rose two point three kilos on insulin.
issues.problem: These weight figures assume everyone stayed on treatment, the same measure as s3. The narration doesn't say so, but the attribution does. It's still consistent because s3 already said it, so this is minor.
issues.fix: Optional, and it keeps the count at 170: "Weight dropped seven and a half to almost thirteen kilos across tirzepatide doses. It rose two point three kilos on insulin." Keep the 'if everyone stayed on treatment' attribution on the s4 stat card.

issues.problem: The trial tested one insulin, degludec, not insulin in general. The on-screen text is slightly broader than the trial.
issues.fix: Change on_screen_text to: "Tirzepatide vs insulin degludec: 1 year"

issues.claim: Stomach side effects were mostly mild to moderate.
issues.problem: This is accurate. The source says gastrointestinal events were generally mild to moderate. But the card shows a 12–24% range without the per-dose split, and the 10 mg arm was 23%.
issues.fix: Add to the s5 attribution: "Nausea 12% / 23% / 24% on 5 / 10 / 15 mg vs 2% on degludec."

issues.problem: The canonical Lancet URL returned 403 to the automated fetcher. The article exists, so this only matters for link checks.
issues.fix: Keep the Lancet URL and add the PubMed record as a backup: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34370970/
